analysis.one_liner: Boosts oil, gas, coal, and nuclear production while raising home energy aid and efficiency standards.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on this bill, but nearly everything in it became law four months later through a different energy bill.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the House Energy and Commerce Committee's version of the Energy Policy Act of 2005. It authorizes research, loan guarantees, and permitting help for oil, gas, coal, nuclear, and ethanol; extends the nuclear industry's accident liability cap; repeals a 1935 law that limited utility holding companies; and mandates renewable fuel in gasoline. It also raises low-income heating assistance to $5.1 billion a year, expands weatherization, sets federal building efficiency targets, and extends daylight saving time.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies get easier access to federal land, streamlined permitting for liquefied natural gas terminals, refinery revitalization zones, and a hydraulic fracturing provision. Coal plant developers get federal loan guarantees and clean coal grants. Nuclear operators get an extended federal liability backstop under the Price-Anderson amendments. Corn and ethanol producers get a nationwide renewable fuel mandate and construction grants. Electric utilities get repeal of the Public Utility Holding Company Act. Low-income households get LIHEAP funded at $5.1 billion a year, weatherization eligibility raised to 150% of poverty, and appliance rebates. Consumers also get new efficiency standards for appliances and buildings, net metering and smart metering rights, and FTC rules against 'slamming' and 'cramming' by electric sellers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Energy producers, utilities, and low-income households

how_it_helps.text: Raises the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program authorization from $2 billion to $5.1 billion per year and raises weatherization eligibility from 125% to 150% of the poverty line [S3].
Requires federal buildings to cut energy use per square foot by 20% by fiscal 2015, mandates energy-efficient procurement, and extends daylight saving time by four weeks [S3].
Requires electric utilities to offer net metering and smart metering on consumer request and lets the FTC ban 'slamming' and 'cramming' of electricity customers [S2].
Mandates renewable fuel (ethanol) in motor vehicle fuel nationwide and authorizes grants and loan guarantees for ethanol and cellulosic biofuel facilities [S2].
Creates refinery revitalization zones with expedited permitting and eases LNG terminal approval, aimed at expanding fuel supply and refining capacity [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund roughly $5.1 billion a year in heating assistance plus clean coal, nuclear, hydrogen, and biofuel programs. The bill shifts more nuclear accident liability onto a capped industry pool rather than full private liability, makes oil and gas drilling on federal land easier to appeal-proof, shields fuel makers from some state fuel rules and groundwater claims through a 'fuels safe harbor,' and gives MTBE producers transition aid. Consumers bear the residual costs of fuel additive contamination and of maintaining the production incentives.

drawbacks.text: The bill extends the Price-Anderson nuclear liability cap, leaving a large share of catastrophic nuclear accident costs with the public rather than plant operators [S2].
It provides transition assistance to MTBE producers and a 'fuels safe harbor' even as MTBE groundwater contamination cases were spreading, and lets the president void the MTBE ban entirely [S2].
It repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, removing long-standing restrictions on utility consolidation in exchange for weaker FERC book-and-records oversight [S2].
The production incentives for oil, gas, coal, and nuclear are authorized at the same time the bill does little to raise vehicle fuel economy standards, which it leaves to a study [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer and low-income provisions are real: heating aid nearly triples, weatherization expands, and appliance and building efficiency standards save money over time. But the bill's center of gravity is production incentives for the largest energy industries — loan guarantees for coal gasification, liability protection for nuclear, drilling and refinery permitting relief, and an ethanol mandate — with the public picking up subsidy costs and contamination risk rather than sharing directly in the gains. As a trade, it leans toward the industries that helped write it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee and sat on the House calendar until the Congress ended without a floor vote — but its substance became law anyway through a separate Senate-amended energy bill that August.

narrative.text: Joe Barton introduced the bill on April 14, 2005, with 14 Republican cosponsors [S1].
It was referred to seven House committees and more than a dozen subcommittees [S5].
The Energy and Commerce Committee reported it amended on July 29, 2005 (H. Rept. 109-215), the other six committees were discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S5].
No House floor vote ever occurred; the action record ends at the calendar, and the Congress expired January 3, 2007 [S5].

The Energy Policy Act of 2005 nonetheless became law in August 2005 (P.L. 109-58) through H.R. 6, the House-passed bill that the Senate amended as the vehicle — a version that, after Senate resistance, dropped the MTBE liability safe harbor that this House bill contained.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Energy producers, utilities, and the ethanol industry came out ahead: their incentives, mandates, and liability provisions became law through the alternate vehicle, and the House-only MTBE safe harbor was the main item they lost. Low-income households also gained from the higher heating-assistance funding that survived into the enacted law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy producers, utilities, and ethanol makers

for.name: Joe Barton
for.role: Chairman, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through his committee to a July 29, 2005 report and placement on the House calendar

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor after it was placed on the Union Calendar, because the chamber had already passed its own energy bill in April 2005

against.name: Senate opponents of the MTBE liability safe harbor
against.what_they_did: Forced removal of the MTBE safe harbor from the final energy law that carried this bill's substance

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were House Republicans; the broader floor fight over the substance played out in the Senate vehicle, H.R. 6, where the MTBE safe harbor was stripped.

industries.note: The bill eases hydraulic fracturing oversight, speeds permitting for LNG terminals and refineries, and opens federal land to leasing — expanding supply but shifting environmental risk toward the public [S2].
The Price-Anderson amendments extend the federal liability backstop and cap industry assessment for catastrophic accidents, keeping costs of a severe nuclear accident partly with the public [S2].
Clean Coal Power Initiative grants and loan guarantees for coal gasification projects channel federal money into coal plants; the public pays the subsidy while sharing in cleaner generation [S2].
A national renewable fuel mandate guarantees ethanol demand regardless of price, plus facility grants and loan guarantees — a permanent revenue channel for farm-state producers [S2].

Repeal of the 1935 Public Utility Holding Company Act frees utilities to consolidate, while new reliability standards, net metering, and FTC anti-slamming rules impose consumer protections on them [S2].

Transition assistance to switch MTBE plants to other fuels, a fuels safe harbor against some litigation, and a presidential waiver option soften the mandated phase-out of a fuel additive linked to groundwater contamination [S2].
New federal efficiency standards and Energy Star procurement requirements create guaranteed demand for efficient appliances, transformers, and lighting [S3].
